   122	\section{Dimension and Unit Parameters}
   123	\seclabel{dimunitparams}
   124	
   125	\begin{Grammar}
   126	\emph{StaticParam} &::=& \KWD{dim} \emph{Id} \\
   127	&$|$& \KWD{unit} \emph{Id} \options{\EXP{\mathrel{\mathtt{:}}} \emph{Type}}
   128	 \options{\KWD{absorbs} \KWD{unit}}\\
   129	\end{Grammar}
   130	
   131	
   132	Static parameters may include one or more \KWD{dim} and \KWD{unit}
   133	parameters.  Syntactically, a \KWD{dim} parameter begins with
   134	\KWD{dim} followed by an identifier.
   135	A \KWD{unit} parameter begins with \KWD{unit}
   136	followed by an identifier, optionally followed by the token `\EXP{\COLONOP}'
   137	and a dimension, and the unit is thereby restricted to be a unit of
   138	the specified dimension.
   139	A \KWD{unit} parameter may include the clause
   140	``\EXP{\KWD{absorbs}\;\KWD{unit}}''; the meaning of this is described
   141	in \secref{absorbing-units}.
   142	A \KWD{dim} parameter is allowed to appear in any context that a
   143	dimension can appear.
   144	A \KWD{unit} parameter is allowed to appear in any context that a unit
   145	can appear.
   146	
   147	
   148	For example, here is a function (in this case actually a prefix operator definition) that is parameterized with a unit:
   149	\note{I manually added a space before U -- Sukyoung}
   150	%opr SQRT[\unit U\](x: RR64 U^2): RR64 U = numericalsqrt(x/U^2) U
   151	\begin{Fortress}
   152	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\surd}\llbracket\KWD{unit}\:U\rrbracket(x\COLON \mathbb{R}64\ U^{2})\COLON \mathbb{R}64\ U = \VAR{numericalsqrt}(x/U^{2})\:U\)
   153	\end{Fortress}
   154	
   155	
   156	\section{Operator Parameters}
   157	\seclabel{opr-ident}
   158	\begin{Grammar}
   159	\emph{StaticParam} &::=& \KWD{opr} \emph{Op} \\
   160	\end{Grammar}
   161	
   162	Static parameters may include one or more operator names.
   163	Syntactically, an operator parameter begins with
   164	\KWD{opr} followed by an operator name.
   165	
   166	
   167	Operator parameters may be freely intermixed with other
   168	static parameters.  For example, the following trait \TYP{IdentityOp}:
   169	\input{\home/basic/examples/StatParam.Opr.IdentityOp.tex}
   170	is parameterized with a type parameter \VAR{T} and
   171	an operator parameter \EXP{\odot}.
   172	Unlike other static parameters,
   173	operator parameters may be used in both type context and
   174	value context.  The operator parameter \EXP{\odot}
   175	is declared as the second static parameter of \TYP{IdentityOp},
   176	instantiated as a static argument in
   177	%IdentityOp[\T,ODOT\]
   178	\EXP{\TYP{IdentityOp}\llbracket{}T,\odot\rrbracket}
   179	which is the bound of \VAR{T},
   180	and declared as an operator method in \TYP{IdentityOp}.
   181	If a trait or object has an operator parameter \OPR{OP} and uses \OPR{OP}
   182	in an expression, then the trait or object must declare or inherit
   183	at least one operator method for \OPR{OP} of matching fixity.
   184	(That is because it would be impossible to type-check \VAR{T}
   185	with any global definition for \OPR{OP},
   186	because the actual operator name is not known
   187	yet, and a definition has to come from somewhere.)
   188	
   189	
   190	Operator parameters are instantiated with operators.
   191	They may be used to instantiate other operator parameters
   192	and the names of operator declarations.
   193	For example, the following trait \TYP{MyIdentity}:
   194	\input{\home/basic/examples/StatParam.Opr.MyIdentity.tex}
   195	instantiates the operator parameter of its supertrait \TYP{IdentityOp}
   196	with the operator name \OPR{IDENTITY}.  It inherits the \OPR{IDENTITY}
   197	operator from \TYP{IdentityOp}.
   198	Two restrictions apply to instantiations of operator parameters:
   199	1) If a trait or object \VAR{T} has operator parameters \EXP{\OPR{OP}_{1}} and
   200	\EXP{\OPR{OP}_{2}}, and \VAR{T} declares or inherits operator methods of the same
   201	fixity for both \EXP{\OPR{OP}_{1}} and \EXP{\OPR{OP}_{2}},
   202	then the actual operators passed in any instantiation of \VAR{T} must
   203	be different.
   204	(That's because it would be impossible to type check any code
   205	in trait \VAR{T} that uses either \EXP{\OPR{OP}_{1}} or
   206	\EXP{\OPR{OP}_{2}} in an expression if such
   207	aliasing were not forbidden.)
   208	Note that the clause ``of the same fixity'' allows both \EXP{\OPR{OP}_{1}} and
   209	\EXP{\OPR{OP}_{2}} to be given the same actual operator, say ``\EXP{-}'',
   210	if \EXP{\OPR{OP}_{1}} has only a prefix definition and \EXP{\OPR{OP}_{2}} has
   211	only an infix definition; this is desirable.
   212	2) If a trait or object \VAR{T} has an operator parameter \OPR{OP} and
   213	declares or inherits an operator method for \OPR{OP},
   214	and also declares or inherits an operator method of the same fixity for
   215	any actual operator \EXP{@} (that is, where \EXP{@} is not an operator
   216	parameter), then the actual operator passed for the \OPR{OP} parameter
   217	must not be \EXP{@}.
   218	(That's because it would be impossible to type check any code
   219	in trait \VAR{T} that uses the operator \EXP{@} in an expression if such
   220	aliasing were not forbidden.)
   221	
   222	
   223	Note that any declarations that may be associated with an actual operator name
   224	that is passed for an operator parameter are \emph{irrelevant} to the behavior
   225	of the operator parameter within the parameterized trait, object, or functional.
   226	When a trait or object extends a trait parameterized by operator names,
   227	the subtrait inherits methods whose names are the actual operator names instead
   228	of the operator parameter names.
   229	
   230	
   231	An operator method declaration whose name is one of the operator parameters
   232	of its enclosing trait or object may be overloaded with other operator
   233	declarations in the same component; the operator parameter may be instantiated
   234	with any operator in the same component.  Therefore, such an operator method
   235	declaration must satisfy the overloading rules
   236	(described in \chapref{multiple-dispatch}) with every operator declaration
   237	in the same component.
   238	For example, the above \OPR{IDENTITY} operator declaration is overloaded
   239	with the following \OPR{IDENTITY} operator declaration:
   240	%opr IDENTITY(x: ZZ) = x
   241	%opr +(x: ZZ) = x
   242	\begin{Fortress}
   243	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{IDENTITY}}(x\COLON \mathbb{Z}) = x\)\\
   244	\(\KWD{opr} +(x\COLON \mathbb{Z}) = x\)
   245	\end{Fortress}
   246	where both \OPR{IDENTITY} and \EXP{+} are top-level operator declarations
   247	in the same component.
   248	Therefore, the declaration of the operator \EXP{\odot} in \TYP{IdentityOp}
   249	must satisfy the overloading rules with \OPR{IDENTITY} and with \EXP{+}.
   250	
   251	
   252	Here are the things programmers can do with an operator parameter:
   253	\begin{enumerate}
   254	\item[(1)] Use it as the defined name in an operator declaration.
   255	    This is what trait
   256	%BinaryOperator[\T,ODOT\]
   257	\EXP{\TYP{BinaryOperator}\llbracket{}T,\odot\rrbracket}
   258	(described in \secref{opr-properties}) does.
   259	
   260	\item[(2)] Pass it as an actual operator to another trait that takes
   261	     an operator parameter.  This is what
   262	\EXP{\TYP{Associative}\llbracket{}T,\odot\rrbracket}
   263	(described in \secref{opr-properties}) does when it extends
   264	\EXP{\TYP{BinaryOperator}\llbracket{}T,\odot\rrbracket}.
   265	
   266	\item[(3)] Use it to distinguish various objects.
   267	    This is what
   268	\EXP{\TYP{Identity}\llbracket\odot\rrbracket}
   269	(described in \secref{opr-properties}) does.
   270	
   271	\item[(4)] Use it as an operator in an expression.
   272	    To do this, an operator declaration for that operator parameter
   273	    must be accessible at the ponit of use, and for that to
   274	    happen, the parameterized trait must either declare
   275	    an operator method with that operator parameter as the name,
   276	    as in case (1), or inherit such a declaration, and the
   277	    only way to do the latter is to use case (2).
   278	\end{enumerate}
   279	
   280	Many interesting examples are described in \secref{opr-properties}.
   281	
   282	
   283	
   284	\section{Where Clauses}
   285	\seclabel{where-clauses}
   286	
   287	\note{The \KWD{where} clause syntax in this section is out of date.}
   288	
   289	\begin{Grammar}
   290	\emph{Where} &::=& \KWD{where} \{ \emph{WhereClauseList} \}\\
   291	\emph{WhereClauseList} &::=& \emph{WhereClause}(\EXP{,}
   292	\emph{WhereClause})$^*$ \\
   293	\emph{WhereClause} &::=& \emph{Id} \emph{Extends}\\
   294	&$|$& \emph{TypeAlias} \\
   295	&$|$& \emph{NatConstraint} \\
   296	&$|$& \emph{IntConstraint} \\
   297	&$|$& \emph{BoolConstraint} \\
   298	&$|$& \emph{UnitConstraint} \\
   299	&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{coerces} \emph{TypeRef}\\
   300	&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{widens} \emph{TypeRef}\\
   301	\end{Grammar}
   302	
   303	
   304	Static parameters may have constraints placed on them
   305	in a \KWD{where} clause.
   306	A \KWD{where} clause begins with
   307	\KWD{where}, followed by a sequence of static
   308	parameter constraints enclosed in braces \EXP{\{} and \EXP{\}},
   309	and separated by commas.
   310	
   311	
   312	A \KWD{where} clause may introduce new static variables, i.e., identifiers
   313	for types and other static entities that may not be static parameters.
   314	We use the term \emph{\KWD{where}-clause variables} to refer to
   315	static variables that are not also static parameters.
   316	The \KWD{where}-clause variables must be bound in a \KWD{where} clause.
   317	
   318	
   319	A static parameter constraint is one of the following forms:
   320	\begin{itemize}
   321	\item a trait constraint consisting of the identifier of
   322	a naked type variable, followed by \KWD{extends}
   323	followed by a set of trait references which may include naked type variables,
   324	\item a type alias (described in \secref{type-alias}),
   325	\item an arithmetic constraint,
   326	\item a boolean constraint,
   327	\item a unit equality constraint,
   328	\item a \KWD{coerces} constraint (described in
   329	  \secref{coercion-declarations}), or
   330	\item a \KWD{widens} constraint (described in
   331	  \secref{coercion-declarations}).
   332	\end{itemize}
   333	A \KWD{where} clause may include mutually recursive constraints.
   334	All static variables in a trait, object, or functional declaration must
   335	occur either as a static parameter or as a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
   336	\appref{where-calculus} describes a Fortress core calculus with
   337	\KWD{where} clauses.
   338	
   339	Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of
   340	themselves. For example, we can write:
   341	%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
   342	%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
   343	%end
   344	\begin{Fortress}
   345	\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
   346	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
   347	\(\KWD{end}\)
   348	\end{Fortress}
   349	In this declaration, for every subtype \VAR{S} of \VAR{T}, \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket}
   350	is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}. Effectively, we have expressed
   351	  the fact that the static parameter \VAR{S} of \VAR{C} is covariant.
   352	
   353	
   354	Trait declarations need not have any static parameters in order
   355	to have a \KWD{where} clause. For example, the following trait
   356	declaration is legal:
   357	%trait C extends D[\T\]
   358	%  where {T extends Object}
   359	%end
   360	\begin{Fortress}
   361	\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{extends} D\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
   362	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
   363	\(\KWD{end}\)
   364	\end{Fortress}
   365	In this declaration, trait \VAR{C} is a subtrait of \emph{every}
   366	instantiation of parametric trait \VAR{D}. Thus, trait \VAR{C} has all
   367	of the methods of every instantiation of \VAR{D}. By thinking of the
   368	declaration this way, we can see what restrictions we need to impose on
   369	the trait \VAR{C} in order for it to be sensible. If trait
   370	\VAR{C} inherits a method declaration that refers to \VAR{T}, it really
   371	contains infinitely many methods (one for each instantiation of \VAR{T}).
   372	However, instantiations of the \KWD{where}-clause variables are not
   373	explicit from the program text as static parameters are.
   374	It must be possible to infer which method is referred to at the call site.
   375	%%So every method invocation is annotated with static types by type inference.
   376	If there is not enough information to infer which method is called,
   377	type checking rejects the
   378	program and requires more type information from the programmer.
   379	Programmers always can provide more type information by using type
   380	ascription as described in \secref{type-ascription}.
   381	
   382	
   383	Object or functional declarations may include \KWD{where} clauses.
   384	Here is an example declaration of an \TYP{Empty} list:
   385	%object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}
   386	%  first() = throw Error
   387	%  rest() = throw Error
   388	%  cons(x) = Cons(x,self)
   389	%  append(xs) = xs
   390	%end
   391	\begin{Fortress}
   392	\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Empty} \KWD{extends} \TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{where} \{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\\
   393	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{first}() = \;\KWD{throw} \TYP{Error}\)\\
   394	\(  \VAR{rest}() = \;\KWD{throw} \TYP{Error}\)\\
   395	\(  \VAR{cons}(x) = \TYP{Cons}(x,\KWD{self})\)\\
   396	\(  \VAR{append}(\VAR{xs}) = \VAR{xs}\)\-\\\poptabs
   397	\(\KWD{end}\)
   398	\end{Fortress}
   399	where \TYP{Cons} is declared in \secref{object-decls}.

    12	\section{Type Inference for Components}
    13	\seclabel{type-inference-components}
    14	
    15	Type inference for Fortress has been described as a procedure performed
    16	over a whole Fortress program in \chapref{type-inference}. In this
    17	section, we explain how this procedure can 
    18	be adapted to perform type inference over a simple program component. 
    19	For a compound component,
    20	concatenate all declarations of all constituents in
    21	the order specified by the constructing \shellcommand{link}
    22	operation.  Constituent compound component declarations are
    23	recursively concatenated.
    24	
    25	
    26	Type inference over a simple component $C$ is performed by first
    27	expanding $C$ into a self-contained Fortress program, as follows:
    28	\begin{enumerate}
    29	\item All program constructs corresponding to declarations in APIs exported by
    30	$C$ are expanded so that they include all types and static parameters
    31	included in the exported APIs. 
    32	\item All types provided by all declarations in the APIs imported by $C$
    33	are prepended to $C$. Note that these declarations must include
    34	types for all variables, functions, fields, and methods;
    35	otherwise the APIs that declare them are not well-formed.
    36	\item In order for the resulting expanded program to be well-formed, 
    37	we assume that all declarations in these APIs are
    38	expanded into special definitions that include \emph{empty bodies}.
    39	The empty body of such a definition is a conceptual body which
    40	cannot be expressed directly in Fortress programs.
    41	Because declarations in APIs do not have any elided type,
    42	type inference ignores empty bodies.
    43	\end{enumerate}
    44	Once $C$ is expanded, type inference 
    45	is performed over all program constructs that still include elided types.
    46	Empty bodies are ignored.

    12	\section{Static Expressions}
    13	\seclabel{static-expr}
    14	
    15	\note{Static expressions are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	\emph{Static expressions} denote \emph{static values}.  Conceptually,
    18	a static expression is not evaluated while a program is running, and
    19	thus its evaluation
    20	cannot complete abruptly.  Given instantiations of all static
    21	parameters (described in \chapref{trait-parameters}) in scope of a
    22	static expression, the value of the static expression can be
    23	determined statically.  Static expressions which use a restricted subset of operations can occur as
    24	\emph{static arguments} which instantiate static parameters and
    25	\KWD{where}-clause constraints (described in \secref{where-clauses}).
    26	We define the set of static
    27	expressions by first defining the types of static expressions, and
    28	distinguishing static values from the closely related literal values.
    29	We then describe the expressions that evaluate to the various kinds of
    30	static values.
    31	
    32	
    33	\subsection{Types of Static Expressions}
    34	
    35	There are three groups of traits that describe literals
    36	and static expressions:
    37	\begin{enumerate}
    38	\item The \emph{literal} traits, which describe boolean,
    39	  character, string, and numerals.  For example, the literal \VAR{true} has
    40	  trait \EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket} and a
    41	  character literal has trait \TYP{Character}.
    42	See \secref{literals} for a discussion of Fortress literals.
    43	
    44	\item The \emph{constant} traits, which describe values denoted by
    45	expressions composed from literals and operators (described in
    46	\secref{constant-values});
    47	the type of a constant expression encodes the value of the expression.
    48	For example, the type of a constant expression \EXP{3+5},
    49	%IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]
    50	\EXP{\TYP{IntegerConstant}\llbracket\VAR{false}, 3+5\rrbracket},
    51	encodes the value of the expression; the operator \EXP{+} is
    52	used in the static arguments.  When an operator is not supported in static
    53	arguments, \library\ can still encode the value of the expression by
    54	providing a specific constant trait such as
    55	\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}
    56	(described in \secref{pi}).
    57	
    58	
    59	
    60	\item The \emph{static} traits, which describe values denoted by
    61	expressions composed from literals, operators (described in
    62	\secref{constant-values}), and \KWD{bool}, \KWD{nat},
    63	and \KWD{int} parameters; here the type
    64	does not encode the value of the expression, but the value of the
    65	expression can nevertheless be known statically if specific
    66	values are specified for the static parameters.  Also, in situations
    67	where the type of an expression composed solely from literals and
    68	operators nevertheless cannot be described by a constant trait, then a
    69	static trait may be used to describe it instead.
    70	For example, a static expression \EXP{2(3+m)} where \VAR{m} is a
    71	\KWD{nat} parameter has trait \TYP{NaturalStatic}.
    72	\end{enumerate}
    73	
    74	
    75	The only operation on literals that produces a new literal (as opposed
    76	to a constant) is concatenation by using the operator \EXP{\|}.
    77	One may concatenate mixed string and
    78	character literals, producing a string literal.
    79	For example, ``\txt{foo}''\EXP{\|}''\txt{bar}'' yields ``\txt{foobar}''.
    80	One may also concatenate two natural numerals
    81	of the same radix, producing a new natural numeral of that radix.
    82	For example, \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16} \| \mathtt{0de}_{16}} yields \EXP{\mathtt{deadc0de}_{16}}.
    83	
    84	Every literal trait extends an appropriate constant trait, and every
    85	constant trait extends an appropriate static trait.  So every
    86	literal is also a constant expression, and every constant expression
    87	is a static expression.
    88	
    89

    91	
    92	\subsection{Static Expressions and Values}
    93	\seclabel{constant-values}
    94	
    95	Static parameters are static expressions.
    96	A \KWD{nat} parameter denotes a value that has type \TYP{NaturalStatic}
    97	(which extends \TYP{IntegerStatic}).
    98	An \KWD{int} parameter denotes a value that has type \TYP{IntegerStatic}.
    99	A \KWD{bool} parameter denotes a value that has type \TYP{BooleanStatic}.
   100	
   101	
   102	Boolean static expressions may be combined using the operators
   103	\EXP{\wedge}, \EXP{\vee}, \EXP{\oplus},
   104	\EXP{\equiv}, \EXP{\leftrightarrow}, \OPR{NAND}, \OPR{NOR}, \EXP{=},
   105	\EXP{\neq}, and \EXP{\rightarrow} (See \appref{operator-precedence} for a
   106	discussion of Fortress operators.)
   107	to produce other static expressions denoting boolean static expressions.
   108	If both operands are boolean constant expressions, then the result is also
   109	a boolean constant expression.
   110	
   111	Character static expressions may be compared using the operators \EXP{<},
   112	\EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, \EXP{>},
   113	\EXP{=}, and \EXP{\neq} to produce boolean static expressions.  If both
   114	operands are character constant expressions, then the result is a boolean
   115	constant expression.
   116	
   117	Numeric static expressions may be compared using the operators \EXP{<},
   118	\EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, \EXP{>},
   119	\EXP{=}, and \EXP{\neq} to produce boolean static expressions.  If both
   120	operands are numeric constant expressions, then the result is a boolean
   121	constant expression.
   122	
   123	Numeric static expressions may be combined using the operators and
   124	functions \EXP{+},
   125	\EXP{-}, \EXP{\times}, \EXP{\cdot}, \EXP{/}, \EXP{!}, \OPR{MIN}, \OPR{MAX},

   131	expressions, then the result is also a numeric constant expression
   132	as long as the constant traits provided by \library\ can encode the value

rule, it is necessary to guess, compute, or pluck from thin air a substitution $\sigma$
that validates the judgment in a type context in which type parameters $\setb{P}$ have been added.

but can be a significant source of inefficiency at run time.  We now make a series of observations.

The function $\msavname$ can be implemented in more than one way.  Rule \rncite{MSAV-Standard} in Figure~\ref{fig:msa}
defines it in a straightforward manner: the most specific of the applicable procedures that are visible.
Rule \rncite{MSAV-Alternate} at the bottom of the same figure takes an alternate approach: the determination of
whether one procedure is more specific than another can be done statically, and the No Duplicates Rule
ensures that there are no cycles in the relationship (therefore ````more specific'' is a partial order).
So the set of methods visible at any call site can be statically sorted, using a topological sort,
into an ordered list such that if procedure 1 is more specific than procedure 2 then procedure 1 appears earlier in the list than procedure 2.
Then all $\msavname$ needs to do at run time is to find the first method in this sorted list that is applicable.

\begin{abstract}

The Fortress programming language integrates traditional mathematical
notation into an object-oriented framework based on traits with
multiple inheritance, overloading (of both methods and functions)
resolved by symmetric dynamic dispatch, static types, and separately
compiled modules.  One innovation is
\emph{functional methods}, which (like conventional ``dotted methods'')
are declared within traits and may be inherited, but are invoked by
ordinary function calls (or mathematical operator syntax) rather
than conventional ``dotted method calls,'' and therefore compete
in overloading resolution with ordinary function declarations.
A component/API system governs visibility of traits, objects, and
functions, and allows separate compilation of components.

A longstanding problem with multiple inheritance is what to do when
methods inherited from several parents conflict.  Many approaches have
been explored in the literature; most fail to obey the
intuitively desirable requirement that the function or method invoked
be the uniquely most specific one that is both accessible and
applicable.  Fortress requires that the signatures in every overload
set form a meet-bounded lattice; therefore it is impossible for any
function or method call to be ambiguous.  This idea goes back nearly
two decades, but Fortress appears to be the first programming language
to adopt and statically enforce it.  Because this rule guarantees
confluence, it enables a distributed implementation of dispatching
that allows selective export and selective optimization.

We exhibit a source-to-source rewrite from a source language
(a stripped-down version of Fortress) to a related target language
that is simpler than the Java\texttrademark\ programming language and is readily
supported by the Java Virtual Machine.  The demonstrated rewriting is
a practical basis for separate compilation and is easily extended to
explicitly type-parameterized methods and functions.

\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
This is a write-up of the theory behind enforcing the return type rule
during runtime type instantiation in the Fortress programming language.
The enforcement of this rule is required for type safety.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

The Fortress programming language has support for symmetric multiple dispatch
over overloaded generic functions and methods.  Unlike many of today's languages with generics, 
Fortress does not follow a type erasure semantics.  Instead
generic type information is recorded at runtime, allowing dispatch decisions to be made
based on generic types.  The price that we must pay for keeping this additional information
is that in order to select a generic function during dispatch, we must choose an applicable
and typesafe instantiation of that generic function.

Elsewhere, we have developed an algorithm and syntactic restrictions on type parameters
to generic functions that supports relatively efficient determination of an applicable instantiation
of a generic function if one exists.  However, the algorithm does not currently enforce the
return type rule which guarantees that the type of the object returned by the chosen instantiation
is a subtype of the type of the function call given by static checking.  The static component of the
return type rule provides strong guarantees about the existence of an instantiation that is both
applicable and type safe if an applicable instantiation exists.  To enforce it at runtime, extra type
variable bounds are needed.  These can be added to and evaluated with the
bounds needed to check applicability without changing which function definition will be chosen.
